newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rent riots erupt in Johannesburg suburbs.
newsitem.headline: Rent riots erupt in Johannesburg suburbs.

text.p: South African police fired rubber bullets and teargas at stone-throwing demonstrators in Johannesburg on Thursday as protests about rates payments descended into riot.

Army units were called in to help quell violence reminiscent of street protests that marked the anti-apartheid past but which have been rare in the country's industrial capital since Nelson Mandela became president after all-race elections in 1994.

Witnesses said several people were wounded by rubber bullets and teargas canisters in the clashes, in predominantly coloured (mixed-race) southern suburbs between the black township of Soweto and the city's downtown business district.
At least one policeman, wounded in a hail of stones and bottles, was also rushed to hospital, a police spokesman said.
"People have a right to peaceful protest but when others are intimidated and life and property put at risk, it is our duty to intervene," said Superintendent Govindsamy Mariemuthoo of Soweto police.
"The situation is very volatile and tense. The South African National Defence Force has come in to assist the police in maintaining law and order and removing barricades."

Hundreds of chanting residents blocked roads with piles of burning tyres and trash cans, protesting against local council threats to evict those who do not pay for the water and electricity they use, and demanding to pay only a flat rate.
The demonstrations were organised by the largely coloured South Western Joint Civics Association, Sowejoca, which called on people to stay away from work to show support.

Passing motorists were jeered at and stoned in Eldorado Park, Westbury and other affected suburbs, public transport was disrupted, schools closed, and council services such as refuse collection were abandoned in other parts of the city.
Rates and rent boycotts were a favoured means of protest against white rule by South Africa's blacks, coloureds and Asians, all classed as separate racial groups under apartheid.
The boycott culture has persisted despite the end of apartheid and Mandela's exhortations for people to pay up and help build a new South Africa.

Worse for cash-strapped councils, the practice has actually spread -- last year whites in Johannesburg's rich northern suburb of Sandton joined in, saying rate hikes of up to 200 percent are outrageous.
"The whites are paying nothing, in Sandton even they are paying nothing -- so what about us?" Sowejoca spokesman Michael Billings said.

Some of the new South Africa's worst street clashes hit Cape Town last year when anti-drug vigilantes, also from the coloured community, declared war on local drug dealers, even torching one to death in front of police.

Such street riots, along with rampant violent crime, have dented South Africa's image abroad. Political analysts say they hope Mandela will take a tough line against violence when he opens parliament on Friday.
